Headline insight: While the national average HSC GPA of 4.01 appears healthy, the data reveals a system under stress. Nearly two-thirds of students (62.6%) scored lower on HSC than on SSC, indicating a widespread performance drop between secondary and higher-secondary levels. The modest +0.018 GPA Progression Delta is driven by a slight improvement from Previous GPA, not from SSC. Regional disparities are substantial: Barisal outperforms Rangpur by 0.20 GPA points (effect size d = 0.34), and the share of students scoring below 3.5 ranges from 20.8% in Dhaka to 32.5% in Rangpur.

GPA Progression: A System Under Stress

The longitudinal GPA data tells a powerful story. Average Previous GPA was 3.99, rising to 4.26 at SSC, then falling back to 4.01 at HSC. The net change from Previous GPA to HSC is a marginal +0.018, but this masks two opposing forces:

  • 50.7% of students improved from their Previous GPA to HSC.
  • 48.4% declined over the same period.
  • 62.6% scored lower on HSC than on SSC — a decline from the immediately preceding exam.
Critical finding: The SSC-to-HSC drop is the most alarming signal in the dataset. It suggests that whatever factors boost performance at SSC (coaching intensity, exam familiarity, curriculum alignment) are not sustained into HSC. Policymakers should investigate curriculum difficulty jumps, teaching quality at the higher-secondary level, and student motivation trajectories.

Socio-Economic Factors and Their Impact on Performance

This section examines family income, parent education, internet access, and private tuition — the levers most often discussed in education policy. The data reveals that parent education produces the largest and most consistent effect, while income, internet, and tuition show surprisingly small associations with HSC outcomes.

Parent Education: The Strongest Predictor

Students whose parents completed secondary education outperform those with primary-educated parents by 0.086 GPA points (Cohen's d = 0.146). The hierarchy is clear: Secondary > Higher Secondary > Graduate > Primary. Notably, graduate-level parent education does not confer additional benefit over secondary — a pattern that merits further qualitative investigation.

Effect-size interpretation: A Cohen's d of 0.146 is small but non-trivial in policy terms. At the population level, shifting a cohort from primary to secondary parent-education exposure could lift hundreds of students into the Good or Excellent tiers.

Internet Access & Private Tuition: Modest Gains

Both internet access and private tuition are associated with higher HSC GPAs, but the effect sizes are minimal:

  • Internet access: +0.017 GPA (d = 0.029) — essentially negligible.
  • Private tuition: +0.012 GPA (d = 0.020) — also negligible.
  • Both together vs neither: +0.030 GPA (d = 0.052) — still small.

The four support-profile groups are remarkably tightly clustered (range 3.99–4.02). This suggests that in the current Bangladeshi context, simply having internet or tuition is not a decisive performance driver. Quality of use (how students utilise internet resources, or the calibre of tuition received) likely matters far more than binary access.

Family Income: No Clear Gradient

Family income shows no linear relationship with HSC performance. The highest-performing income quartile is Q3 (mean 4.025), not Q4 (4.012). The overall range across quartiles is only 0.033 GPA points (d = −0.018), indicating that income alone does not determine academic success in this sample.

Policy implication: If income and binary resource access show such weak links to outcomes, interventions should focus on how resources are used (pedagogical quality, digital literacy, parental engagement) rather than whether they are available.

Study Behavior and Attendance Patterns

Conventional wisdom holds that more study hours and higher attendance should boost results. The Bangladesh dataset partially challenges this assumption.

Study Hours: Non-Linear and Weakly Negative

The correlation between weekly study hours and HSC GPA is −0.022 — essentially zero. Students studying 0–10 hours per week average 4.03, while those studying 16–20 hours average 3.95. The pattern is U-shaped rather than linear: moderate study loads (16–20 hours) underperform both lighter and heavier loads.

Attendance: No Predictive Power

Attendance correlates with HSC GPA at −0.014. Students in the 76–85% attendance bracket actually score highest (4.07), while those with near-perfect attendance (96–100%) score lowest (3.94). This counter-intuitive finding suggests that:

  • Attendance may be a poor proxy for engagement in this context.
  • Students with lower attendance may compensate with more focused self-study or private tuition.
  • School quality (what happens in class) may matter more than simply being present.
Key takeaway: Policy should move beyond "butt-in-seat" metrics. Targeted, high-quality instruction and effective self-study strategies are likely more impactful than simply increasing study hours or enforcing attendance.

Regional Performance Disparities

Geographic inequality is the most pronounced dimension in the dataset. The gap between the highest-performing district (Barisal, 4.113) and the lowest (Rangpur, 3.909) is 0.204 GPA points (d = 0.34). This is the largest effect size observed across any single factor.

District × School Type Heatmap

The interaction between district and school type reveals institutional inequalities that are not uniform. In Dhaka, public schools dramatically outperform private schools (+0.233 GPA). In Rajshahi, the reverse is true (−0.173 in favour of private). These divergences suggest that "public vs private" is not a universal quality signal — local governance, funding, and teacher quality likely drive the difference.

Excellent Performance & Below-3.5 Rates by District

Barisal leads in excellent performance (36.8%) and maintains a relatively low below-3.5 rate (21.6%). Rangpur trails on both metrics: only 20.3% excellent and 32.5% below 3.5. Chattogram also shows a high below-3.5 rate (27.1%) despite a middling average, indicating a polarised distribution.

GPA Progression Delta by District

Rajshahi (+0.078) and Dhaka (+0.058) show the strongest improvement from Previous GPA to HSC, suggesting effective higher-secondary systems. Rangpur (−0.057) and Sylhet (−0.029) are the only districts with negative deltas, indicating systemic decline between academic stages.

SSC-to-HSC Decline by District

Nationally, 62.6% of students scored lower on HSC than SSC. The decline is steepest in Sylhet (66.7%) and Rangpur (65.9%), and mildest in Barisal (54.4%) and Rajshahi (59.0%). Districts with lower decline rates tend to have higher absolute HSC performance, reinforcing the interpretation that these regions have stronger higher-secondary ecosystems.

Gender and School-Type Gaps by District

Gender gaps are small overall (female mean 4.023 vs male 4.002, d = 0.037) but directionally inconsistent across districts. Males outperform females in Dhaka, Rajshahi, and Barisal; females lead in Mymensingh, Khulna, Sylhet, and Chattogram. The public–private gap is similarly heterogeneous: public schools lead in Dhaka, Sylhet, and Barisal, while private schools lead in Rajshahi and Khulna.

Key Findings and Policy Recommendations

Synthesised Findings

  1. Regional disparity is the dominant inequality. The Barisal–Rangpur gap (0.204 GPA, d = 0.34) dwarfs socio-economic and gender gaps. District-level governance, teacher deployment, and resource allocation should be the top policy priority.
  2. The SSC-to-HSC decline is systemic. Six in ten students perform worse on HSC than SSC. This points to a curriculum or pedagogy shock at the higher-secondary transition, not individual student failure.
  3. Parent education matters more than income or resource access. Binary markers (internet, tuition) show negligible effects. The home learning environment — proxied by parent education — is the strongest household-level predictor.
  4. Attendance and study hours are weak predictors. Near-zero correlations suggest that quality of engagement, not quantity, drives outcomes.
  5. Public vs private performance is context-dependent. In some districts public schools excel; in others, private schools do. Blanket privatisation or public-expansion policies are unlikely to work without local diagnostics.

Actionable Recommendations

1. Launch a district-targeted HSC transition support programme

Prioritise Rangpur, Khulna, and Mymensingh — the three districts with the lowest HSC means and highest below-3.5 rates. Fund bridge courses between SSC and HSC, focusing on mathematics, science, and English where curriculum jumps are typically steepest. Target the 62.6% of students who decline from SSC to HSC with diagnostic assessments at the start of HSC Year 1.

2. Invest in parental engagement and literacy programmes

Since parent education shows the largest household-level effect, scale adult literacy and "learning at home" campaigns in districts with high shares of primary-educated parents (notably Rangpur and Khulna). Even modest lifts in parental academic engagement can shift student performance at the population level.

3. Shift from access metrics to quality metrics for digital and tuition interventions

Internet access and private tuition show negligible returns in their current form. Rather than subsidising connectivity or tutoring indiscriminately, pilot "quality-assured" models: curated digital learning platforms, tutor certification schemes, and structured homework support. Measure impact via randomised controlled trials before national scale-up.

4. Redesign attendance and study-hour monitoring

Replace raw attendance targets with classroom-engagement indices (student participation, assignment completion, formative assessment scores). Similarly, guide students toward evidence-based study techniques (spaced practice, retrieval quizzes) rather than simply increasing study hours.

5. Conduct district-level institutional audits

The reversal of public–private performance across districts (e.g., Dhaka public > private; Rajshahi private > public) implies that governance, teacher quality, and school leadership vary more by location than by sector. Commission independent audits of school management, teacher absenteeism, and classroom observation scores in the bottom-three and top-three districts to identify replicable practices.

6. Maintain gender-equity monitoring

Although the national gender gap is small, directional reversals across districts warrant continued surveillance. Ensure that any district-targeted intervention does not inadvertently widen gender disparities — for example, by scheduling bridge courses at times that conflict with female students' domestic responsibilities.
